title: Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc. (1996)
summary: The federal trial court had to apply New York’s damages-excessiveness standard, while federal appellate review remained limited by the federal jury-trial structure.
notes:
This case illustrates why “apply state substantive law and federal procedure” requires further analysis. The labels alone do not determine which standard and which reviewing institution control.

Gasperini, a journalist, had lent 300 original slide transparencies that the Center lost; the jury awarded $1,500 per slide, the district court denied a new trial, and the Second Circuit ordered a new trial unless he accepted a remittitur to $100,000; the Supreme Court (Ginsburg, J., 5–4) vacated and remanded for the district judge to apply New York's 'deviates materially' standard.

sections.Parties: Gasperini sought compensation from the Center for Humanities for photographic transparencies that were lost after being supplied for use.
sections.Material Facts: The jury valued the missing images and returned a substantial damages award. New York law used a standard asking whether an award materially deviated from reasonable compensation. The federal system also had its own allocation of functions among jury, trial judge, and appellate court. The dispute therefore involved both the substantive effect of controlling excessive awards and the institutional method of review.
sections.Procedural History: The federal jury awarded $450,000. Appellate proceedings reduced the permissible award. The Supreme Court remanded with instructions that accommodated the state standard through the federal trial judge, with appellate review for abuse of discretion.
sections.Issue: How should a federal diversity court reconcile New York’s standard for reviewing excessive damages with federal jury-trial and appellate-review constraints?
sections.Holding: The state standard was to be applied by the federal district judge, and the court of appeals was to use the constrained abuse-of-discretion review appropriate to that determination.
sections.Reasoning: The state standard affected the size of recoveries and thus the practical content of the state-law remedy. Disregarding it could produce materially different awards simply because the case was in federal court. At the same time, direct appellate reexamination of jury findings raised a distinct federal constitutional concern. The Court sought to give effect to both sets of interests by allocating application of the state standard to the district court under the federal new-trial structure, while limiting the appellate court’s role. The analysis therefore depends on both the standard selected and the decision-maker applying it.

learning.why: The federal trial court had to apply New York’s damages-excessiveness standard, while federal appellate review remained limited by the federal jury-trial structure.

topics.cp-erie-accommodation: The Court accommodated the state damages-review standard within the federal allocation of trial and appellate functions. The trial judge had to apply the state materially-deviates standard described in the opinion.
topics.cp-judge-jury: The Seventh Amendment affected how federal appellate courts reviewed the jury verdict.
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: Gasperini assigns the state excessiveness standard to the federal trial court, with appellate review for abuse of discretion protecting the allocation of fact-review authority.
topics.cp-erie-balancing: The majority relied on Byrd's balancing of state interests against the federal judge-jury allocation and the Seventh Amendment's Reexamination Clause.
topics.cp-rule-scope: The Scalia dissent argued Rule 59 covered the point, making the threshold Hanna question central to the disagreement.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Scalia, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice Thomas, viewed Federal Rule 59 as controlling and objected to the accommodation. Justice Stevens also disagreed with aspects of the Court’s disposition.
